title: The beasts (Revelation 13)
hook: empire as a beast demanding worship; many read 666 as a code for Nero

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman clothed with the sun, a dragon thrown down, and the earth swallowing a flood. Your line was the dragon loses. Which mother did you help or hold in mind? Day one thousand three hundred five.

Six hundred threescore and six. Those words have set off a great deal of guessing. They come from one verse at the end of Revelation thirteen. But before the number, there's a crowd. A beast has risen out of the sea, and the whole world is following it in wonder. People are bowing down. And they're chanting a question, the kind of question you shout at a rally: "Who is like unto the beast? who is able to make war with him?" Today's word is that beast, and the one that comes after it.

First, the chant is borrowed. After the sea crossing in Exodus, Moses and Israel sang: "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?" The crowd in Revelation takes a song meant for God and sings it to a beast. That's the beast's whole project: to be worshiped. It's given power, the text says, over every kindred and tongue and nation. Second, a second beast. This one comes up out of the earth, and the description is chilling: "he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon." It looks gentle. It sounds like something else. Its job is to make everyone worship the first beast, and to see that no one can buy or sell without its mark. Third, the number. The text says: "Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man." Readers have tried their hand at it. Some readers hear a code for Nero, the Roman emperor. Others read it as a symbol: a number that keeps falling short. Others again wait for a figure still to come. The text itself only says it is the number of a man. Fourth, what John says to do about it. Not panic, not decode. In the middle of the chapter: "Here is the patience and the faith of the saints." Some readers carry the chapter into ordinary life this way: the beast need not look like a monster. It can be any power that asks for more than loyalty, that wants worship. And it can look like a lamb.
screen: `A SONG FOR GOD, SUNG TO A BEAST.`
`HORNS LIKE A LAMB, VOICE OF A DRAGON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where power demands worship. Settle, and breathe. Think over the last week. Where did something ask for more of you than it should? A company that wants your whole evening. A screen that wants your attention every few minutes. A leader, a party, a crowd that asks you never to question it. Don't judge yourself. Just see it plainly, the way John saw a lamb's horns and heard a dragon's voice. If you pray, you can name it to God and give your loyalty back where you believe it belongs. If you don't, just name it to yourself. The bell holds the time.
The beasts. In Revelation thirteen, one from the sea that wants worship, and one from the earth that looks like a lamb and speaks like a dragon.
Your line: don't bow to the beast. Today, when something demands all of you, say no to it once, gently and on purpose, and notice that you still can. Day one thousand three hundred five.

howItsDone: Christians read Revelation 13 in different ways: some as a word about Rome in John's own day, some as a pattern that repeats whenever power asks to be worshiped, and some as a picture of events still to come.

original.note: Greek: a wild beast, the word for both creatures in Revelation 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: 666 is a secret code for a villain at the end of the world.
what it means: a power that demands worship, and a second, lamb-like power that sells it to everyone.
what a scholar hears: "who is like unto the beast?" parodies the song at the sea in Exodus 15, and the beast takes what belongs to God.

notes: The index hook says 'many read 666 as a code for Nero'; the script softens this to 'some readers' under the strict claims rule. The gematria (Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters) and the 616 variant are left out deliberately.
Nero is named only as the Roman emperor; no history of his reign is claimed.
Three readings of the number (Nero; symbol of falling short; a future figure) given without ranking. Confirm fair.
Practice examples (employer, screens, a party or crowd) are meant generally and name no real party or leader.
Editor pass: 'counted ever since' cut (unsourced); the closing 'the beast is rarely a monster... often looks like a lamb' recast as some readers' application, not the narrator's claim.
